questions.answer: The same global mean forcing can produce different regional climate responses because aerosol location, absorption characteristics, and atmospheric adjustments influence circulation and precipitation patterns.
author: Ken Carslaw
options: Their temperature responses must be identical everywhere
Their regional precipitation responses may differ substantially
Their forcing efficacies must be identical
Their cloud responses must be identical

questions.prompt: Which of the following aerosols most strongly causes a fast precipitation response and why?
questions.answer: Black carbon aerosol most strongly causes a fast precipitation response because it heats the atmosphere. The fast 'forcing-driven' precipitation response to a change in aerosol occurs without any change in surface temperature (by definition). Heating of the atmosphere, which is very fast, above an unchanged surface stabilises the atmosphere and reduces water vertical transport and precipitation. An alternative explanation is that atmospheric heating from black carbon is balanced by a reduction in latent heating of the atmosphere from water condensation in order to restore atmospheric energy balance. See section 2.5.3 for more discussion on this topic.
author: Ken Carslaw
options: Secondary organic aerosol because it cools the land surface
Black carbon because it heats the atmosphere
Sulphate aerosol because it most strongly affects cloud droplet concentrations
Sea spray aerosol because it strongly affects planetary albedo

questions.prompt: Why did the introduction of Effective Radiative Forcing (ERF) improve comparisons among forcing agents?
questions.answer: ERFs take into account atmospheric adjustments. Adjustments are processes that occur on timescales faster than the surface temperature response. For aerosols these are mostly changes in cloud properties, which alter the instantaneous radiative forcing caused by changes in atmospheric radiation and cloud droplet concentrations. This 'adjusted' or effective forcing is what causes the change in temperature, so neglecting them meant that temperature responses were not so comparable across forcing agents. Note that such adjustments don't apply just to aerosols; changes in carbon dioxide can also cause cloud adjustments, as explained in the book. See Box 2.2 and related text.
author: Ken Carslaw
options: It removed several sources of model uncertainty
It removes cloud effects, which were a major source of uncertainty
It includes atmospheric adjustments occurring before surface warming
It measures forcing at the top of the atmosphere rather than at the top of the stratosphere

questions.prompt: Two climate models reproduce the observed 20th-century warming equally well. Model A has a strongly negative aerosol forcing, while Model B has a weaker aerosol forcing. What is the most likely implication?
questions.answer: Model A probably has a higher climate sensitivity. Model A has a strongly negative aerosol radiative forcing, which will offset a larger fraction of the greenhouse gas forcing over the industrial period. Model A therefore has a smaller positive forcing than model B. For model A to simulate the same change in temperature over the industrial period as model B, it must have a higher climate sensitivity (\(dT/dF\)) to cause the same \(\Delta T\) with a smaller \(\Delta F\). See section 2.3.5.
author: Ken Carslaw
options: Model A probably has a lower climate sensitivity
Model A probably has a higher climate sensitivity
Aerosol forcing does not influence temperature simulations
Future temperature projections of the two models will be very similar

questions.prompt: (Needs improvement. Each question needs a 'because...' and the decoys could be better). A climate policy successfully removes anthropogenic aerosol emissions over 20 years and carbon dioxide emission rates stabilise. Which outcome is most likely?
questions.answer: Removal of aerosol emissions over 20 years would remove the negative aerosol radiative forcing that are are currently causing. Stabilisation of carbon dioxide emissions would cause atmospheric concentrations to still increase, albeit more slowly. The net effect would be an acceleration of warming.
author: Ken Carslaw
options: Gradual global cooling
No climatic response
Acceleration of warming as aerosol masking is removed
Rapid decrease in climate sensitivity

questions.prompt: An Arctic stratus cloud has a cloud droplet number concentration \(N_\mathrm{d}\) of 20 cm\(^{-3}\). A subtropical cumulus cloud \(N_\mathrm{d}\) = 120 cm\(^{-3}\). A parcel of dry air containing 20 cm\(^{-3}\) of aerosol is entrained into the cloud. Assuming all these aerosols act as CCN and nucleate, the total liquid water content of the cloud is approximately constant, and that within a cloud, the droplets are of the same size, calculate:
questions.answer: Reflectivity scales with \(\sqrt[3]{N_\mathrm{d}}\). To calculate the fractional change, we can do \(\sqrt[3]{\frac{N_\mathrm{old}+N_\mathrm{new}}{N_\mathrm{old}}}\), where \(N_\mathrm{old}\) is the droplet number before the entrainment and \(N_\mathrm{new}\) is the droplet number after the entrainment.
